claim: Animals use temporal information from previously experienced periodic events to instruct their future behaviors.
source: Animals use the temporal information from previously experienced periodic events to instruct their future behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the research context.

claim: The retina and cortex are involved in using temporal information from periodic events for behavior.
source: The retina and cortex are involved in such behavior, but it remains largely unknown how the thalamus, transferring visual information from the retina to the cortex, processes the periodic temporal patterns.
evidence: This statement references existing knowledge about retina and cortex involvement without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: It remains largely unknown how the thalamus processes periodic temporal patterns.
source: The retina and cortex are involved in such behavior, but it remains largely unknown how the thalamus, transferring visual information from the retina to the cortex, processes the periodic temporal patterns.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Luminance cells in the nucleus dorsolateralis anterior thalami (DLA) of pigeons exhibited oscillatory activities in a temporal pattern identical to rhythmic luminance changes of repetitive light/dark stimuli with durations in the seconds-to-minutes range.
source: Here we report that the luminance cells in the nucleus dorsolateralis anterior thalami (DLA) of pigeons exhibited oscillatory activities in a temporal pattern identical to the rhythmic luminance changes of repetitive light/dark (LD) stimuli with durations in the seconds-to-minutes range.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: After LD stimulation, DLA cells retained the entrained oscillatory activities with an interval closely matching the duration of the LD cycle.
source: Particularly, after LD stimulation, the DLA cells retained the entrained oscillatory activities with an interval closely matching the duration of the LD cycle.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding demonstrated in multiple figures.

claim: The post-stimulus oscillatory activities of DLA cells were sustained without feedback inputs from the pallium.
source: Furthermore, the post-stimulus oscillatory activities of the DLA cells were sustained without feedback inputs from the pallium (equivalent to the mammalian cortex).
evidence: This finding is supported by pharmacological inactivation and lesion experiments.

claim: Experience-dependent representation of time interval in the brain might not be confined to the pallial/cortical level, but may occur as early as at the thalamic level.
source: Our study suggests that the experience-dependent representation of time interval in the brain might not be confined to the pallial/cortical level, but may occur as early as at the thalamic level.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Use of perceived temporal information from previously experienced stimuli to predict upcoming events has been demonstrated in birds.
source: Use of the perceived temporal information from previously experienced stimuli to predict upcoming events has been demonstrated in birds (Gibbon et al., 1984; Henderson et al., 2006; Kalenscher et al., 2006), rodents (Crystal and Baramidze, 2007; Agostino et al., 2011), primates, and humans (Leon and Shadlen, 2003; Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Janssen and Shadlen, 2005; Penney et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Use of perceived temporal information from previously experienced stimuli to predict upcoming events has been demonstrated in rodents.
source: Use of the perceived temporal information from previously experienced stimuli to predict upcoming events has been demonstrated in birds (Gibbon et al., 1984; Henderson et al., 2006; Kalenscher et al., 2006), rodents (Crystal and Baramidze, 2007; Agostino et al., 2011), primates, and humans (Leon and Shadlen, 2003; Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Janssen and Shadlen, 2005; Penney et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: Use of perceived temporal information from previously experienced stimuli to predict upcoming events has been demonstrated in primates and humans.
source: Use of the perceived temporal information from previously experienced stimuli to predict upcoming events has been demonstrated in birds (Gibbon et al., 1984; Henderson et al., 2006; Kalenscher et al., 2006), rodents (Crystal and Baramidze, 2007; Agostino et al., 2011), primates, and humans (Leon and Shadlen, 2003; Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Janssen and Shadlen, 2005; Penney et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to primate and human studies.

claim: Previous studies on the neural mechanism underlying time perception and representation have mainly focused on the cerebellum.
source: Previous studies on the neural mechanism underlying time perception and representation have mainly focused on the cerebellum (Malapani et al., 1998; Harrington et al., 2004), striatum (Meck et al., 2008; Mello et al., 2015), and cortex of humans and mammals (Leon and Shadlen, 2003; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cerebellum studies.

claim: Previous studies on the neural mechanism underlying time perception and representation have mainly focused on the striatum.
source: Previous studies on the neural mechanism underlying time perception and representation have mainly focused on the cerebellum (Malapani et al., 1998; Harrington et al., 2004), striatum (Meck et al., 2008; Mello et al., 2015), and cortex of humans and mammals (Leon and Shadlen, 2003; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to striatum studies.

claim: Previous studies on the neural mechanism underlying time perception and representation have mainly focused on the cortex of humans and mammals.
source: Previous studies on the neural mechanism underlying time perception and representation have mainly focused on the cerebellum (Malapani et al., 1998; Harrington et al., 2004), striatum (Meck et al., 2008; Mello et al., 2015), and cortex of humans and mammals (Leon and Shadlen, 2003; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cortex studies.

claim: Some retinal ganglion cells in salamander and mouse retinae signal the time at which an omitted stimulus in a sequence of flashes would occur.
source: A recent study showed, however, that some retinal ganglion cells in salamander and mouse retinae signal the time at which an omitted stimulus in a sequence of flashes would occur (Schwartz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The visual thalamus filters, rather than passively relays, the visual information sensed by the retina as it signals to the cortex.
source: There is also increasing evidence showing that the visual thalamus filters, rather than passively relays, the visual information sensed by the retina as it signals to the cortex (Cudeiro and Sillito, 2006; Saalmann and Kastner, 2011; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The pigeon is a common animal model for behavioral and neurobiological studies of time-dependent cognitive tasks.
source: The pigeon is a common animal model for behavioral and neurobiological studies of time-dependent cognitive tasks, such as interval timing (Kalenscher et al., 2006), sequence learning (Helduser et al., 2013; Lissek et al., 2013), and delayed matching-to-sample (Browning et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using pigeons.

claim: Birds have developed a complex visual system that is superior to that of most vertebrates.
source: Furthermore, to achieve foraging and safe flight successfully in diverse environments, birds have developed a complex visual system that is superior to that of most vertebrates (Shimizu and Watanabe, 2012; Wylie et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The avian DLA receives direct retinal inputs.
source: The avian DLA receives direct retinal inputs, projects onto the pallial Wulst in both hemispheres (Karten et al., 1973; Bagnoli and Burkhalter, 1983; Miceli et al., 1987, 2008), and receives feedback inputs from the pallial Wulst (Karten et al., 1973; Miceli et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The avian DLA projects onto the pallial Wulst in both hemispheres.
source: The avian DLA receives direct retinal inputs, projects onto the pallial Wulst in both hemispheres (Karten et al., 1973; Bagnoli and Burkhalter, 1983; Miceli et al., 1987, 2008), and receives feedback inputs from the pallial Wulst (Karten et al., 1973; Miceli et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The avian DLA receives feedback inputs from the pallial Wulst.
source: The avian DLA receives direct retinal inputs, projects onto the pallial Wulst in both hemispheres (Karten et al., 1973; Bagnoli and Burkhalter, 1983; Miceli et al., 1987, 2008), and receives feedback inputs from the pallial Wulst (Karten et al., 1973; Miceli et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The avian retina-DLA-Wulst pathway is comparable to the mammalian retina-lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)-striate visual pathway.
source: The avian retina-DLA-Wulst pathway is comparable to the mammalian retina-lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)-striate visual pathway (Shimizu and Karten, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The avian Wulst projects onto the nidopallium caudolaterale (NCL).
source: The avian Wulst further projects onto the nidopallium caudolaterale (NCL), which is comparable to the mammalian prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The avian nidopallium caudolaterale (NCL) is comparable to the mammalian prefrontal cortex (PFC).
source: The avian Wulst further projects onto the nidopallium caudolaterale (NCL), which is comparable to the mammalian prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Luminance cells in the pigeon DLA can encode ambient luminance.
source: More importantly, the luminance cells in the pigeon DLA can encode ambient luminance (Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: During visual conditioning, the responses of DLA luminance cells to the conditioned stimulus are modified by training.
source: During visual conditioning, the responses of the DLA luminance cells to the conditioned stimulus (CS: whole-field light) are modified by training, and the training-induced changes that occur in response to the CS are in parallel with the acquisition of the behavioral responses of pigeons (Gibbs et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Training-induced changes in DLA luminance cell responses to the conditioned stimulus are in parallel with the acquisition of behavioral responses of pigeons.
source: During visual conditioning, the responses of the DLA luminance cells to the conditioned stimulus (CS: whole-field light) are modified by training, and the training-induced changes that occur in response to the CS are in parallel with the acquisition of the behavioral responses of pigeons (Gibbs et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: 190 DLA luminance cells were recorded from 19 animals.
source: We recorded 190 DLA luminance cells from 19 animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: DLA luminance cells encoded ambient luminance and sustained steady activities under constant photic conditions.
source: These cells encoded ambient luminance and sustained steady activities under constant photic conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: DLA luminance cells' firing rates either increased (light-activated) or decreased (light-suppressed) monotonically when the luminance level of the stimulus was raised in steps.
source: Their firing rates either increased (light-activated) or decreased (light-suppressed) monotonically when the luminance level of the stimulus was raised in steps (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: During LD stimulation, all luminance cells synchronized their firing rates with the rhythmic luminance changes of LD stimuli whose temporal frequencies ranged from 0.5 Hz to 0.002 Hz.
source: During LD stimulation, all luminance cells synchronized their firing rates with the rhythmic luminance changes of LD stimuli whose temporal frequencies ranged from 0.5 Hz (L/D: 1 s/1 s) to 0.002 Hz (L/D: 240 s/240 s).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The oscillation frequencies of the entrained activities of luminance cells were closely correlated with the temporal frequencies of the luminance changes of LD stimuli (linear regression, slope = 0.99, R2 = 0.99).
source: The oscillation frequencies of the entrained activities of these cells were closely correlated with the temporal frequencies of the luminance changes of LD stimuli (linear regression, slope = 0.99, R2 = 0.99).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: 54 cells (28%) retained the entrained oscillatory activities under constant photic conditions after LD stimulation.
source: We found that 54 cells (54/190 = 28%) retained the entrained oscillatory activities under constant photic conditions after LD stimulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Replay cells included 25 light-activated and 29 light-suppressed cells.
source: Thus, these cells were referred to as replay cells, which included 25 light-activated and 29 light-suppressed cells.
evidence: This is a classification of the recorded cells based on experimental data.

claim: 136 DLA cells (72%) displayed non-oscillatory response patterns after LD stimulation and were referred to as non-replay cells.
source: The remaining DLA cells (136/190 = 72%) displayed non-oscillatory response patterns after LD stimulation and were therefore referred to as non-replay cells.
evidence: This is a classification of the recorded cells based on experimental data.

claim: Replay cells did not exhibit oscillatory activities after LD stimulation when the duration of the LD cycle was shorter than 10 s.
source: We found that, first, replay cells did not exhibit oscillatory activities after LD stimulation when the duration of the LD cycle was shorter than 10 s (L/D: 5 s/5 s).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The oscillation frequencies of replay cells (n = 54 cells) after LD stimulation were highly correlated with the temporal frequencies of LD stimuli (slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.99).
source: The oscillation frequencies of replay cells (n = 54 cells) after LD stimulation were highly correlated with the temporal frequencies of LD stimuli (slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.99) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Once a replay cell returned to its steady non-oscillatory activity under constant photic conditions, it could be re-entrained by visual stimuli of other frequencies.
source: Furthermore, once a replay cell returned to its steady non-oscillatory activity under constant photic conditions, it could be re-entrained by visual stimuli of other frequencies (6 cells, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The duration of the first replay cycle after LD stimulation was linearly correlated with the duration of the LD cycle (slope = 0.58, R2 = 0.95, n = 54 cells).
source: The duration of the first replay cycle after LD stimulation was also linearly correlated with the duration of the LD cycle (slope = 0.58, R2 = 0.95, n = 54 cells) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The increase in the number of LD cycles led to an increase in the oscillation time of replay cells after LD stimulation.
source: Second, the increase in the number of LD cycles led to an increase in the oscillation time of replay cells after LD stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: When the temporal frequency of the LD stimulus was set to 0.0165 Hz (L/D: 30 s/30 s), the number of replay cycles increased when the number of LD cycles increased (slope = 0.41, R2 = 0.99, n = 21 cells).
source: When the temporal frequency of the LD stimulus was set to 0.0165 Hz (L/D: 30 s/30 s), the number of replay cycles increased when the number of LD cycles increased (slope = 0.41, R2 = 0.99, n = 21 cells) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After LD stimulation, the entrained oscillatory activities of replay cells gradually returned to non-oscillatory activities with time.
source: After LD stimulation, the entrained oscillatory activities of replay cells gradually returned to non-oscillatory activities with time.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The change in replay cell activity over time was reflected in the decrease of oscillation frequency and response amplitude.
source: The change was reflected in the decrease of oscillation frequency and response amplitude.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The duration of the replay cycle slowly increased over time (one-way ANOVA, F5, 180 = 4.38, p < 0.001, n = 31 cells).
source: We observed that the duration of the replay cycle slowly increased over time (one-way ANOVA, F5, 180 = 4.38, p < 0.001, n = 31 cells; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The peak activity of the replay cycle gradually decreased over time (F5, 180 = 3.59, p = 0.004).
source: For the same group of replay cells, the peak activity of the replay cycle gradually decreased over time (F5, 180 = 3.59, p = 0.004) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Wulst inactivation attenuated the spontaneous activities of replay cells.
source: Wulst inactivation attenuated the spontaneous activities of replay cells, but had no effect on their photic responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claim: Wulst inactivation had no effect on the photic responses of replay cells.
source: Wulst inactivation attenuated the spontaneous activities of replay cells, but had no effect on their photic responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claim: The spontaneous firing rates of replay cells were slightly reduced from 3.89 ± 0.87 spikes/s before injection to 2.3 ± 0.51 spikes/s after injection (paired t-test, tpre vs. post = 2.37, p = 0.03, n = 12 cells).
source: Under constant photic conditions before LD stimulation, the spontaneous firing rates of replay cells were slightly reduced from 3.89 ± 0.87 spikes/s (mean ± SEM) before injection to 2.3 ± 0.51 spikes/s after injection (paired t-test, tpre vs. post = 2.37, p = 0.03, n = 12 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the pharmacological inactivation data.

claim: No significant change in the preference index was observed after Wulst inactivation for the light-activated cells (pre-injection: 0.34 ± 0.15; post-injection: 0.5 ± 0.22; Wilcoxon rank sum test, ranksum = 21, p = 0.22, n = 5 cells).
source: No significant change in the preference index was observed after Wulst inactivation for the light-activated cells (pre-injection: 0.34 ± 0.15; post-injection: 0.5 ± 0.22; Wilcoxon rank sum test, ranksum = 21, p = 0.22, n = 5 cells) or for light-suppressed cells (pre-injection: −0.52 ± −0.19; post-injection: −0.43 ± −0.16; ranksum = 46, p = 0.45, n = 7 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the pharmacological inactivation data.

claim: No significant change in the preference index was observed after Wulst inactivation for light-suppressed cells (pre-injection: −0.52 ± −0.19; post-injection: −0.43 ± −0.16; ranksum = 46, p = 0.45, n = 7 cells).
source: No significant change in the preference index was observed after Wulst inactivation for the light-activated cells (pre-injection: 0.34 ± 0.15; post-injection: 0.5 ± 0.22; Wilcoxon rank sum test, ranksum = 21, p = 0.22, n = 5 cells) or for light-suppressed cells (pre-injection: −0.52 ± −0.19; post-injection: −0.43 ± −0.16; ranksum = 46, p = 0.45, n = 7 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the pharmacological inactivation data.

claim: The entrained post-stimulus oscillatory activities of replay cells were still sustained when the Wulst was temporarily inactivated.
source: The entrained post-stimulus oscillatory activities of replay cells were still sustained when the Wulst was temporarily inactivated, as shown for a single replay cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither the linear correlation between the post-stimulus oscillation frequencies of replay cells and the temporal frequencies of LD stimuli (pre-injection: slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.92; post-injection: slope = 0.56, R2 = 0.82) was significantly affected by Wulst inactivation.
source: Neither the linear correlation between the post-stimulus oscillation frequencies of replay cells and the temporal frequencies of LD stimuli (pre-injection: slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.92; post-injection: slope = 0.56, R2 = 0.82; Figure 4A) nor the linear correlation between the duration of the first replay cycle and the duration of the LD cycle were significantly affected by Wulst inactivation (pre-injection: slope = 0.59, R2 = 0.91; post-injection: slope = 0.73, R2 = 0.96; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The linear correlation between the duration of the first replay cycle and the duration of the LD cycle was not significantly affected by Wulst inactivation (pre-injection: slope = 0.59, R2 = 0.91; post-injection: slope = 0.73, R2 = 0.96).
source: Neither the linear correlation between the post-stimulus oscillation frequencies of replay cells and the temporal frequencies of LD stimuli (pre-injection: slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.92; post-injection: slope = 0.56, R2 = 0.82; Figure 4A) nor the linear correlation between the duration of the first replay cycle and the duration of the LD cycle were significantly affected by Wulst inactivation (pre-injection: slope = 0.59, R2 = 0.91; post-injection: slope = 0.73, R2 = 0.96; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: After Wulst inactivation, the replay cells could still be re-entrained by periodic stimuli of different frequencies (n = 4 cells).
source: After Wulst inactivation, the replay cells could still be re-entrained by periodic stimuli of different frequencies (n = 4 cells, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The number of replay cycles increased as the number of LD cycles (30 s/30 s) increased (pre-injection: slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.68; post-injection: slope = 0.54, R2 = 0.64, n = 10 cells).
source: The number of replay cycles increased as the number of LD cycles (30 s/30 s) increased (pre-injection: slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.68; post-injection: slope = 0.54, R2 = 0.64, n = 10 cells) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For the same periodic stimulus, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells before and after injection showed no significant differences in oscillation frequencies (paired t-test, tpre vs. post = 0.32, p = 0.75).
source: In addition, for the same periodic stimulus, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells before and after injection showed no significant differences in oscillation frequencies (paired t-test, tpre vs. post = 0.32, p = 0.75 ; Figure 4A), duration of the first replay cycle (tpre vs. post = –1.71, p = 0.1; Figure 4C), or number of replay cycles (tpre vs. post = –0.94, p = 0.37; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For the same periodic stimulus, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells before and after injection showed no significant differences in duration of the first replay cycle (tpre vs. post = –1.71, p = 0.1).
source: In addition, for the same periodic stimulus, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells before and after injection showed no significant differences in oscillation frequencies (paired t-test, tpre vs. post = 0.32, p = 0.75 ; Figure 4A), duration of the first replay cycle (tpre vs. post = –1.71, p = 0.1; Figure 4C), or number of replay cycles (tpre vs. post = –0.94, p = 0.37; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For the same periodic stimulus, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells before and after injection showed no significant differences in number of replay cycles (tpre vs. post = –0.94, p = 0.37).
source: In addition, for the same periodic stimulus, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells before and after injection showed no significant differences in oscillation frequencies (paired t-test, tpre vs. post = 0.32, p = 0.75 ; Figure 4A), duration of the first replay cycle (tpre vs. post = –1.71, p = 0.1; Figure 4C), or number of replay cycles (tpre vs. post = –0.94, p = 0.37; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The post-stimulus activities of replay cells declined over time before and after injection, which was reflected in the increasing duration of replay cycles (one-way ANOVA, pre-injection: F5, 66 = 4.05, p = 0.002; post-injection: F5, 66 = 4.55, p < 0.0001, n = 12 cells).
source: Furthermore, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells declined over time before and after injection, which was reflected in the increasing duration of replay cycles (one-way ANOVA, pre-injection: F5, 66 = 4.05, p = 0.002; post-injection: F5, 66 = 4.55, p < 0.0001, n = 12 cells; Figure 4E) and decreasing peak responses of replay cycles over time (pre-injection: F5, 66 = 3.17, p = 0.01; post-injection: F5, 66 = 2.94, p = 0.01; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The post-stimulus activities of replay cells declined over time before and after injection, which was reflected in decreasing peak responses of replay cycles over time (pre-injection: F5, 66 = 3.17, p = 0.01; post-injection: F5, 66 = 2.94, p = 0.01).
source: Furthermore, the post-stimulus activities of replay cells declined over time before and after injection, which was reflected in the increasing duration of replay cycles (one-way ANOVA, pre-injection: F5, 66 = 4.05, p = 0.002; post-injection: F5, 66 = 4.55, p < 0.0001, n = 12 cells; Figure 4E) and decreasing peak responses of replay cycles over time (pre-injection: F5, 66 = 3.17, p = 0.01; post-injection: F5, 66 = 2.94, p = 0.01; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Injection of 1 µl of muscimol (2%) can completely inactivate neuronal activities in a 2 mm diameter around the cannula tip for ~3 hr.
source: Injection of 1 µl of muscimol (2%) can completely inactivate neuronal activities in a 2 mm diameter around the cannula tip for ~3 hr, and can significantly attenuate the neuronal activities in a 4 mm diameter (Partsalis et al., 1995; Arikan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Injection of 1 µl of muscimol (2%) can significantly attenuate the neuronal activities in a 4 mm diameter.
source: Injection of 1 µl of muscimol (2%) can completely inactivate neuronal activities in a 2 mm diameter around the cannula tip for ~3 hr, and can significantly attenuate the neuronal activities in a 4 mm diameter (Partsalis et al., 1995; Arikan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 29 replay cells were recorded from nine Wulst-lesioned animals, which included 14 light-activated and 15 light-suppressed cells.
source: We recorded 29 replay cells from nine Wulst-lesioned animals, which included 14 light-activated and 15 light-suppressed cells.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from lesion experiments.

claim: Wulst lesions did not affect the spontaneous activities or photic responses of the DLA replay cells.
source: By comparing the neuronal responses of the DLA replay cells in normal and Wulst-lesioned animals, we found that Wulst lesions did not affect the spontaneous activities or photic responses of the DLA replay cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the lesion experiments.

claim: No significant firing rate changes were observed between the replay cells recorded in the normal animals (3.39 ± 0.43 spikes/s) and those in Wulst-lesioned animals (3.54 ± 0.36 spikes/s) (t-test, tnormal vs. lesion = –0.26, p = 0.39, nnormal = 54 cells, nlesion = 29 cells).
source: Under constant photic conditions before LD stimulation, no significant firing rate changes were observed between the replay cells recorded in the normal animals (3.39 ± 0.43 spikes/s) and those in Wulst-lesioned animals (3.54 ± 0.36 spikes/s) (t-test, tnormal vs. lesion = –0.26, p = 0.39, nnormal = 54 cells, nlesion = 29 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the lesion data.

claim: The photic responses of the DLA replay cells were not affected by Wulst lesions, which was reflected in the comparable preference indices of light-activated cells (normal animals: 0.46 ± 0.06, n = 25 cells; lesion animals: 0.5 ± 0.05, n = 14 cells, t-test, tnormal vs. lesion = –0.46, p = 0.64).
source: Furthermore, the photic responses of the DLA replay cells were not affected by Wulst lesions, which was reflected in the comparable preference indices of light-activated cells (normal animals: 0.46 ± 0.06, n = 25 cells; lesion animals: 0.5 ± 0.05, n = 14 cells, t-test, tnormal vs. lesion = –0.46, p = 0.64) and those of light-suppressed cells (normal animals: −0.52 ± −0.06, n = 29 cells; lesion animals: −0.42 ± −0.03, n = 15 cells, tnormal vs. lesion = -1.38, p = 0.17).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the lesion data.

claim: The photic responses of the DLA replay cells were not affected by Wulst lesions, which was reflected in the comparable preference indices of light-suppressed cells (normal animals: −0.52 ± −0.06, n = 29 cells; lesion animals: −0.42 ± −0.03, n = 15 cells, tnormal vs. lesion = -1.38, p = 0.17).
source: Furthermore, the photic responses of the DLA replay cells were not affected by Wulst lesions, which was reflected in the comparable preference indices of light-activated cells (normal animals: 0.46 ± 0.06, n = 25 cells; lesion animals: 0.5 ± 0.05, n = 14 cells, t-test, tnormal vs. lesion = –0.46, p = 0.64) and those of light-suppressed cells (normal animals: −0.52 ± −0.06, n = 29 cells; lesion animals: −0.42 ± −0.03, n = 15 cells, tnormal vs. lesion = -1.38, p = 0.17).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the lesion data.

claim: The post-stimulus oscillatory activities of replay cells were still retained after the application of Wulst lesions in both hemispheres.
source: The post-stimulus oscillatory activities of replay cells were still retained after the application of Wulst lesions in both hemispheres.
evidence: This is a finding from the lesion experiments.

claim: After LD stimulation, the replay cells still showed oscillatory activities, and the oscillation frequencies were linearly correlated with the temporal frequencies of LD stimuli (slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.99, n = 29 cells).
source: After LD stimulation, the replay cells still showed oscillatory activities, and the oscillation frequencies were linearly correlated with the temporal frequencies of LD stimuli (slope = 0.62, R2 = 0.99, n = 29 cells) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the lesion data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Replay cells (six cells) could be re-entrained by periodic stimuli of different frequencies after Wulst lesions.
source: Furthermore, replay cells (six cells) could be re-entrained by periodic stimuli of different frequencies (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the lesion experiments shown in Figure 5B.

source: Before the injection, the spontaneous firing rates of the Wulst cells surrounding the injection sites were 6.55 ± 0.85 spikes/s (n = 3 injection sites).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: The firing rates of Wulst cells between 0.25 hr and 1.5 hr after injection were only 15.9% ± 3.7% (1.08 ± 0.37 spikes/s) of those before injection.
source: Their firing rates between 0.25 hr and 1.5 hr after injection were only 15.9% ± 3.7% (1.08 ± 0.37 spikes/s) of those before injection, and slowly increased to 26.3% ± 0.3% (1.72 ± 0.22 spikes/s) between 1.5 hr and 3 hr after injection.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: The firing rates of Wulst cells slowly increased to 26.3% ± 0.3% (1.72 ± 0.22 spikes/s) between 1.5 hr and 3 hr after injection.
source: Their firing rates between 0.25 hr and 1.5 hr after injection were only 15.9% ± 3.7% (1.08 ± 0.37 spikes/s) of those before injection, and slowly increased to 26.3% ± 0.3% (1.72 ± 0.22 spikes/s) between 1.5 hr and 3 hr after injection.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: Muscimol effectively inhibited the Wulst cells, but successful Wulst inactivation did not affect the entrained post-stimulus oscillatory activities of the DLA replay cells.
source: Taken together, these data illustrate that muscimol effectively inhibited the Wulst cells, but that successful Wulst inactivation did not affect the entrained post-stimulus oscillatory activities of the DLA replay cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: Projections of the DLA mainly terminate in the HD and HI of the Wulst.
source: Projections of the DLA mainly terminate in the HD and HI of the Wulst (Karten et al., 1973; Bagnoli and Burkhalter, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The HA is the major area of the Wulst that sends projections forward to other visual and somatosensory/motor areas and back to the DLA in the brain.
source: The HA is the major area of the Wulst that sends projections forward to other visual and somatosensory/motor areas and back to the DLA in the brain (Karten et al., 1973; Reiner and Karten, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.
